name: Epicurus
role: Ancient Greek philosopher and founder of the Garden (341–270 BCE)
summary: Epicurus recommended a quiet life centered on friendship, prudent choices and simple needs. He held that justice grew out of agreements for mutual protection and that laws were just insofar as they benefited people in their dealings with one another.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: Principal Doctrines 15 and 26 distinguish limited natural needs from insatiable wants and recommend letting go of unnecessary desires that are hard to satisfy or liable to cause harm. Vatican Sayings 67–68 connect accumulating great wealth with dependence and describe the dissatisfaction of someone who always wants more.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: Principal Doctrine 1 says that blessed and imperishable gods cause trouble for no one, and the Letter to Menoeceus §§123–124 rejects the attribution of human rewards and punishments to them. Principal Doctrines 31–33 ground justice among people in their own agreements.

divinely-chosen-superior-people.rationale: The Letter to Menoeceus §§123–124 denies that the gods dispense benefits and punishments among humans. Principal Doctrine 1 excludes favoritism from the nature of a blessed and imperishable being.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Principal Doctrines 31 and 37 ground just law in mutual protection and actual benefit in people’s dealings, making that benefit the test of justice.

no-duty-to-obey.rationale: Principal Doctrines 33–38 derive justice from mutually beneficial agreements and hold that enactment cannot make an unbeneficial rule just. In the fragment Plutarch attributes to the letter to Idomeneus, Epicurus advises against living in subjection to laws when there is no threat of harm.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Principal Doctrine 12 makes knowledge of nature essential to dispelling fears sustained by myth. In the Letter to Herodotus §§78–81, Epicurus explains celestial events through natural inquiry and identifies belief in their divine governance as a source of fear.

simple-living.rationale: In the Letter to Menoeceus §§127–131, Epicurus recommends training oneself to be content with simple, inexpensive provisions and distinguishes necessary desires from empty ones. Principal Doctrine 15 describes natural wants as limited and easy to satisfy.

unjust-law-not-binding.rationale: Principal Doctrines 37–38 hold that a rule without mutual benefit lacks justice even when the law declares it just. The letter fragment preserved in Against Colotes §34 treats exposure to harm as a reason to heed laws.

withdraw-from-politics.rationale: Diogenes Laertius X.119 attributes to the first book of On Lifecourses the advice that a wise person stays out of politics. Vatican Saying 58 describes withdrawal from public affairs as a release from confinement.

notes: Reviewed economy, government, society, world, liberty, culture, ecology, technology, means and globalism against the letters, doctrines, sayings, fragments and biographical record. The follow-up on government and world looked at kingship, lawmaking, obedience, relations among peoples and war. The Garden’s arrangements describe a school and the will describes an estate. Later Epicureans’ accounts of social development and statecraft were used to locate leads for Epicurus’s own record.
